We had staff who had to be paid to keep maintaining them. “Eventually, when we determined the exact amount needed to complete the project—after President Jonathan intervened and his successor, the late President Muhammadu Buhari, directed his team to resolve the issues arising from the privatization—we were thrilled that Afreximbank stepped in. They shared our vision and understood the impact the project would have on the community. “I believe that was the turning point for them. Seeing Aba’s potential as an industrial hub in Africa made them far more willing to find a way to make the project work. Although subsequent challenges prolonged completion, Afreximbank ultimately came to the rescue. “At that crucial juncture, we needed $50 million, and they provided it. Honestly, Afreximbank’s role in all of this was remarkable. Ordinarily, a bank or financier would walk away from a project facing the kinds of hurdles we had at the time. “We were operating in an environment where the government had breached the terms of our signed agreement. We were dealing with civil and public service officials who knew what needed to be done but refused to act. “There was little to offer them comfort beyond the sheer determination of our lead investor. For him, it wasn’t merely a financial venture; his drive to see the project through was fueled by a desire to create a lasting, positive impact on people’s lives.” Infrastructure built for reliability The company says its investment in distribution infrastructure is central to its efforts to maintain stable electricity supply. According to the Director of Commercial Operations, Engineer Victor Ngwoke, Aba Power deliberately invested in heavy-duty tubular steel poles designed to withstand extreme conditions and minimise disruptions. “We wanted to have a very sturdy and reliable infrastructure. We, therefore, deliberately invested in heavy tubular steel poles,” he said. Ngwoke explained that the poles have deeply buried concrete foundations and are designed to withstand substantial impact, including collisions with vehicles. He said the company also maintained standards for conventional concrete poles and worked to restore damaged infrastructure quickly whenever faults occurred. On metering, the director said approximately 98 per cent of Aba Power’s customers had prepaid meters, helping to reduce disputes associated with estimated billing. With prepaid meters, customers can monitor their consumption and manage electricity expenses more effectively. Ngwoke also disclosed that the company deployed smart meters and monitoring teams to detect and prevent electricity theft, including illegal connections and meter bypasses. He said residents had also supported efforts to protect the network, recognising the benefits of reliable electricity to their businesses and livelihoods. Excess capacity, wider reach Aba Power currently takes an average of 50 to 60 megawatts from an installed generation capacity exceeding 140MW, according to the company. The available capacity has enabled it to extend electricity supply to parts of neighbouring Rivers State, where some communities are underserved by the Port Harcourt Electricity Distribution Company. The company says it hopes to extend its reach across Abia State, subject to the necessary infrastructure and operational requirements. He contacted Nnaji for assistance, and the institution was connected to Aba Power within 48 hours. Before the connection, he said, academic activities, research and other operations were constrained by unreliable electricity, with staff often leaving the campus by 2pm. With the improved supply, students and staff now remain on campus until late in the evening, despite the institution not being residential. “Before now, staff used to leave by 2pm. They cannot work without electricity. You cannot carry out research without electricity,” he said. The rector said the institution’s energy costs had fallen by about 80 per cent. item.title: FG disagrees with World Bank over H1 124% debt servicing/revenue ratio
item.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Federal Government has disagreed with the World Bank on the latter’s debt servicing/revenue ratio for the first half of 2026, put at 124 percent. The bank in its recent Nigeria Development Update (NDU) reported that federal government debt servicing was 124 percent above its revenue. However, the Federal Ministry of Finance, in a statement, yesterday, faulted the bank’s analysis, explaining that the debt servicing figure included those of the state governments and that it was, therefore, wrong to analyse it against the federal government revenue for the period under consideration. The statement read in part, “This conclusion is misleading, for three reasons, the government said. “The interest figure includes debt the Federal Government services on behalf of other tiers of government, including external loans to states. “Measuring this against federal revenue alone overstates the ratio which is only meaningful when debt and revenue cover the same level of government. “The reported revenue is also incomplete. It excludes independent revenue already earned by government agencies and enterprises but not yet remitted to the Treasury. ” In addition, more revenue is typically earned in the second half of the year than in the first due to the statutory timing of certain tax payments. This is why the ratio stood at 156% in H1 2025, while the full-year 2025 debt-service-to-revenue ratio was below 60%, down from 97% before the reforms. ” This is a clear sign of the progress delivered by the current administration’s reforms. “Between the first half of 2025 and the first half of 2026, federal revenue rose by 72%, from ₦3.6 trillion to ₦6.2 trillion. Interest payments rose by a much slower 38%, from ₦5.6 trillion to ₦7.7 trillion. ” Revenue is therefore growing almost twice as fast as interest costs. item.title: FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt
item.description: With the Federal Government’s debts to power generation companies hitting the N6 trillion mark at the end of 2025, the government has gone to the bond market to raise funds to make up for its inability to fund electricity subsidies from the national budget. NERC, in its 2025 industry report, put the Federal Government’s gross tariff subsidy obligation at N1.928 trillion for the year, representing 57.44 percent of the total NBET invoice. The amount translates to an average subsidy obligation of N160.69 billion per month. The government’s subsidy obligation was distributed across the four quarters, with N536.40 billion recorded in the first quarter, N514.36 billion in the second quarter, N458.76 billion in the third quarter and N418.79 billion in the fourth quarter. The 2025 figure represented a slight decline from the N1.949 trillion subsidy obligation recorded in 2024. The government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector. The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies. The Managing Director/CEO, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc, Akin Odeyemi said, at the backdrop of weak growth in power supply the GenCos appear to be shackled by indebtedness by the Federal Government with outstanding debt put around N6 trillion at the beginning of this year. Consequently, the government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector. The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies. Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists Despite concerns over the sector’s performance, the Minister of Power, Mr. Joseph Tegbe, has insisted that electricity supply has improved over the past three months. Tegbe, who acknowledged that some parts of the country continued to experience poor supply, said the government was working to address the challenges. According to him, “Operational record reports show generation and transmission above 5,000MW over the past couple of weeks, compared to the 3,700 to 4,700MW range before June, and a generation peak of 5,330MW during August and September. “Our next task is to sustain these gains and translate them into more dependable supply at customer level. The objective cannot be to preserve the institutions of transition indefinitely. item.title: 2027: I won’t step down for ADC, Kwankwaso declares
item.description: …says party no better than APC By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has ruled out withdrawing from the 2027 presidential race in favour of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, declaring that the opposition party offers no better alternative to the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC. Kwankwaso’s declaration comes amid opposition manoeuvres ahead of the election, with the NDC chieftain accusing the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, of promoting claims that his ticket with Peter Obi is working for the APC or may step down for the ADC candidate at the last minute. In a statement on Sunday, Kwankwaso accused the ADC campaign team of directing unnecessary attacks at him, Obi and the NDC instead of selling its own candidate to Nigerians. “We will not withdraw our candidature for the ADC or any other party,” he declared. Kwankwaso also dismissed suggestions that the NDC ticket was acting on behalf of the ruling party, insisting that it remained committed to contesting the election. “The OK ticket is neither working for nor acting on behalf of the APC or any of its candidates. We see no possibility or reason to withdraw from the presidential race in favour of the ADC candidate or any other,” he said. Turning his attention to the ADC campaign council, Kwankwaso urged it to address allegations levelled against its presidential candidate by Vice-President Kashim Shettima rather than attack the NDC ticket. He also rejected the ADC’s claim to being an alternative to the APC-led government, which he accused of failing Nigerians. “The APC-led government has failed Nigerians. The ADC offers no better alternative,” Kwankwaso declared. Presenting the NDC as a stronger opposition platform, he said his ticket with Obi had the credibility, capacity and nationwide support to unite the country and tackle insecurity, education, agriculture, infrastructure, healthcare and economic challenges. Kwankwaso urged supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to remain committed to the party’s electoral victory, describing the NDC as the country’s most formidable opposition party. “I therefore urge all our supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to continue working toward the victory of our great party,” he said. item.title: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn
item.description: Supply grows by 4.8% Available plant capacity falls by 41% 13 years of privatisation yield little results FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists Consumers, experts react Revenue collected by Nigeria’s electricity Distribution Companies (DisCos) rose by about 450 per cent in eight years, from N218.16 billion in the first half of 2018 to N1.2 trillion in the corresponding period of 2026, far outpacing growth in electricity supply over the period. Data from the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), analysed by Financial Vanguard, showed that while DisCos’ revenue increased by about N983.04 billion, total electricity supply grew by only 4.8 per cent, from 16,861 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first half of 2018 to 17,668GWh in the first half of 2026, even as their debt profile in the last six months hits N700billion. The data also indicated that average available generation capacity declined by 41 per cent, from 7,565.5 megawatts (MW) in the first half of 2018 to 4,456MW in the corresponding period of 2026. On an annual basis, DisCos’ revenue increased by about 666 per cent in ten years, from N302.93 billion in 2016 to N2.32 trillion in 2025, highlighting the widening gap between revenue growth and improvements in electricity supply. NERC data showed that while DisCos’ annual revenue rose by about N2.016 trillion over the period, average daily power generation increased by approximately 36 per cent, from 3,276MW in 2016 to 4,475MW in 2025. The disparity has raised concerns about the extent to which increased revenue collections have translated into improved electricity supply and service delivery to consumers, 13 years after the privatisation of the power sector. In the same vein, data from NERC showed that in the first half of 2026, DisCos failed to collect N700.53 billion. It indicated that while the utilities received N1.9trillion worth of energy from the market, they collected N1.2trillion from consumers, leaving a balance of N700 billion. The Rural Electrification Agency (REA) has estimated that about 85 million Nigerians still lack access to electricity. In 2016, DisCos collected N302.925 billion, while total annual electricity supply stood at 23,742GWh. By 2025, revenue had risen by about 666 per cent to N2.3188 trillion, while annual electricity supply increased by 31.6 per cent to 31,251GWh. DisCos’ revenue rose to N370.456 billion in 2017, before increasing to N448.749 billion in 2019 and N542.729 billion in 2020. Collections further climbed to N775.336 billion in 2021 and N841.811 billion in 2022. The upward trend accelerated in subsequent years, with revenue reaching N1.0775 trillion in 2023, N1.6597 trillion in 2024 and N2.3188 trillion in 2025. By comparison, annual electricity supply increased from 23,742GWh in 2016 to 33,489.17GWh in 2019 and 35,242.17GWh in 2020. It rose further to 36,710.60GWh in 2023 and peaked at 37,093.70GWh in 2024 before declining to 31,251GWh in 2025.

item.title: Despite inflation trend down, stocks sustain losses amid selling pressure
item.description: The Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX dropped further Week-on-Week, WoW, amid selling pressure across sectors despite the fourth consecutive month of decline in headline inflation rate for the month of September 2026. Specifically, the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of equities listed on the Exchange, dropped to N260.725 trillion last Friday from N161.260 trillion the previous week, as investors lost over N535 billion. Similarly, another market gauge, NGX All Share Index, ASI nosedived by 0.3% to close last Friday at 247539.73 points from 248,363.55 points the previous week. Analysis of trading showed that the market closed lower for the third consecutive week, as losses in Zenith Bank by -6 .5%, MTN Nigeria -1.8%, First HoldCo -3.9% and GTCO -4.4% contributed significantly to drag the ASI down WoW, bringing the Month-to-Date, MtD and Year-to-Date, YtD returns to -1.5% and +59.1%, respectively. On market activity, trading volume and value declined by 39.0% WoW and 38.0% WoW, respectively. On sector performance, the Banking declined by -3.1% and Insurance Index -0.1% , while the Oil & Gas Index rose by 3.1% and Consumer Goods 0.1% respectively. The Industrial Goods index closed flat. Commenting on the market outlook, analysts at Cordros Capital Limited, stated: “Looking ahead, we expect market sentiment to improve, supported by bargain hunting following recent price declines. Secondly, anticipation of third quarter, Q3 earnings releases and positioning ahead of upcoming dividend qualification dates, which could drive selective buying interest.” On their part, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, said: “The oil market’s movements may also influence expectations regarding inflation, energy costs and broader economic activity. Changes in crude prices can affect transportation, production and distribution costs, with potential implications for businesses across several sectors. However, the implications for individual companies will vary according to their exposure to energy prices, operating structures and ability to pass higher costs on to customers. Investors should therefore assess the potential impact of oil-price movements within the context of individual company fundamentals and the wider economic environment.” The post Despite inflation trend down, stocks sustain losses amid selling pressure appeared first on Vanguard News .

Abari added that although Kashim came from a political family and held his own political views, he never allowed political differences to damage his relationships with others. The former NOA director-general said the suddenness of the death was a reminder of the uncertainty of human life. “If I recall the moments we had together, I recall the banters, everything. He explained the cause of his disappointment to Economy&Lifestyle, saying: “Before, N1,000 food from Mama Rukayat would fill my stomach completely, gesturing toward his plate. “Now, I spend N1,500 and I leave the table still feeling hungry. “I have to drink two sachets of water right after eating just to feel heavy. It is survival eating. “We are no longer eating to enjoy; we are eating so we don’t collapse.” Mr. Sunday Agbonkhese, a bricklayer, said: “Before, you can get cooked beans (ewa agoyin) and bread with N700. “You will be full. But now, that N700 can hardly get you a loaf of bread to make you full. “To get full now, you will need up to N3,000 for a meal of bread and beans. “After eating this, which is also a small portion, compared to a few years back, I don’t eat for the rest of the day till evening. “I eat twice a day now just to be able to save a little from my earning which is also little. “It is only God that is feeding me.” Why the portions are shrinking Mrs. Kudirat Adeyemi, who has operated a popular food canteen for over 12 years, stares at her large aluminum pots. According to her, a year ago, a single standard scoop of rice alongside a piece of beef cost N800. But today, maintaining that same quantity would require her to charge N2,000; a price her regular customers, mostly motorcycle riders and traders, simply cannot afford. “If I increase the price to what it actually costs to cook this food, nobody will buy. “So, I had to change the strategy. “The price is now N1,200, but the portion is nearly half of what it used to be. “The piece of meat is smaller, and the rice spoon is no longer heaped. “My customers complain bitterly, but they know it is not my fault. “Even sales have reduced because now I cook two rubbers, almost 5 kg of rice compared to 25kg I was cooking before. “The market is hot.” The reality is visible on the plates of her patrons. What used to be a mountain of rice that could sustain a manual laborer for an entire day has shrunk to a modest mound. Customers adapt to survive The reduction in food portions has drastically altered the eating habits of consumers, many of whom have seen their disposable incomes evaporate. With salaries stagnant and the cost of basic commodities tripling, eating has transformed from a convenient necessity into an exercise in strict budgeting. Economists point out that the food vendor crisis is a direct reflection of a deeper macro-economic strain. The cost of a bag of rice, a staple food in Nigerian households, has hit record high ranging from N60,000 to N100,000, while prices of cooking gas, tomatoes, onions, and vegetable oil have followed a similar trajectory. Many food vendors have closed their shops entirely because they lack the capital to restock. For those remaining, portion control is the only alternative to bankruptcy. A food truck owner, Musa Ibrahim opined that reducing quantities is an act of desperation rather than profit-seeking. “Every morning at the market, the prices of ingredients change. A basket of pepper that was N25,000 last week can increase to N35,000 next week. “If the quantity of food on the plate is not reduced, food vendors will be cooking at a loss and we won’t have money to buy ingredients tomorrow. “Our customers’ pockets are dwindling, so we must give them what their money can buy, even if it is just a few spoons.” Until structural changes occur in agriculture, security, f, both vendors and consumers are trapped in a cycle of diminishing returns. For now, the plates at Nigeria’s food stalls will likely remain light, serving as a stark, daily reminder of the economic pressures squeezing the nation’s tables. With no special allocation from the Federal Government to Lagos State for constant infrastructure maintenance and upgrade, the situation appears precarious but, definitely, not completely hopeless. It is not hopeless because the state government keeps thinking out of the box to do its beat and its best within the limit of available resources. These non-stop efforts keep the infrastructure standing despite the unparalleled pressure on them from different angles. In recent times, some Lagosians have been complaining bitterly about the health sector of the state because of some isolated cases in one or two public health facilities. Like the other sectors that are also constantly under pressure, such as education, transportation and housing, among others, the health sector is having its fair share of the pressure. Even with the continued addition of new health facilities, the pressure has not abated, no thanks to the huge population and the national brain-drain epidemic in the health sector. The few available doctors and other health professionals in the system are also under immense pressure, making the situation a tinderbox. These challenges are what many of us Lagosians quite understand, but which the armchair critics, some of whom do not even use the public health facilities, refuse to grasp. Although the World Health Organisation (WHO) has clarified that it does not endorse a single, one-size-fits-all ratio of doctor to patients, because different countries have varying organisational, financial and workforce structures, the Nigerian Association of Resident Doctors (NARD) reports that the actual ratio in Nigeria is roughly one doctor to over 9,000 patients! The ratio may even be worse in Lagos because of the exploding population. In fact, an approximate 15,692 Nigerian-trained medical doctors currently practice in the United Kingdom, being the third highest after Pakistan and India. While the figure is said to be about 20,000 in the United States (U.S), thousands also practice in Canada, France and other European countries. These figures are incredibly high and crippling for Nigeria to grow its near comatose health sector. They have worsened the brain-drain in the country’s health sector. In fact, if not that the Sanwo-Olu administration is always investing in the health sector through infrastructure development, hospital expansion, modernisation of equipment and capacity building for health workers, the sector would have long caved in under pressure from Lagosians. While the government has invested and still continues to invest humongous amounts of money in upgrading all the general hospitals in the state, it newly constructed Massey Street Children’s Hospital on a 4,000 square metres of land, designed to strengthen access to qualify healthcare for children in the state. The hospital is the largest in West Africa. The new Ojo General Hospital is another important addition to the state healthcare infrastructure. It is strategically positioned to improve access to healthcare services for residents of Ojo and the surrounding communities, including the Badagry axis. The government has also embarked on the construction of a major psychiatric healthcare facility in Epe, representing an important investment in mental-health infrastructure and specialised care. Besides, there has been continued development and upgrading of facilities at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH), Ikeja, to strengthen the capacity of the tertiary healthcare institution to provide specialised and advanced medical services. It had earlier embarked on the massive renovation and upgrading of facilities at the General Hospitals in Somolu, Odan-Lagos and Isolo, as well as the Ebute-Meta and Ketu-Ejinrin Health Centres, among several others. It also established 10 Triage and Oxygen Centres and activated the Covid-19 Oxygen Treatment and Sample Collection Centres. It has covered about a million Lagosians under the Health Insurance Scheme, among several other massive investments in the all-important health sector. Not left out in the investment spree is human-capacity development and professional training for health personnel. These investments demonstrate that healthcare development is not limited to building hospitals alone. In fact, under the supervision of the hardworking Commissioner for Health, Professor Akinola Abayomi, Lagos has witnessed a tremendous development in the last seven years of the Sanwo-Olu administration. However, the minor challenges in the health sector in a cosmopolitan state like Lagos should not be interpreted as evidence that the government is doing nothing. Therefore, instead of a very few residents embarking on bitter, destructive, blanket and sweeping criticisms, aimed at diminishing the spirited efforts of the state government, which millions of other Lagosians keep appreciating, it is the duty of everybody to identify and present evidenced-based areas that need improvement and draw the attention of the government to them. Criticism must be objective, constructive and genuine. Once all these conditions are met, Sanwo-Olu and Abayomi, as well as other top members of the administration who have, on several occasions in the past, demonstrated their speed of responsiveness, as can be attested to by this writer, will surely respond to them. According to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, “People’s participation is the essence of good governance.” Governance, therefore, is supposed to be the collective efforts of both the government and the governed. Mr. Steve Omolale, a seasoned journalist, writes from Lagos. The post Lagos and Its Overburdened Health Sector appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.description: Three developments have crossed our reporting threshold this weekend. They concern the All Progressives Congress (APC) expanding political organisation in Kaduna, fresh local-government election results in Kogi, and an increasingly public disagreement between two major opposition presidential campaigns. 1. KADUNA: PROMINENT EL-RUFAI ALLIES RETURN TO APC Kaduna is in the North-West region. Several former associates of ex-Governor Nasir El-Rufai have defected from the ADC to the APC. They include former Chief of Staff and Finance Commissioner Muhammad Bashir Sa’idu, former Education Commissioner Jafaru Sani and former Senator Suleiman Abdu Kwari. Combo Photo of Uba Sani (L) AND Nasir El-Rufai (R) The defections were formally acknowledged at a reception in Zaria on Saturday, October 17. Sa’idu claims that more than 200,000 ADC members and supporters have moved to the APC. That figure remains an unverified political claim, not an independently established membership count. The departures followed disagreements over the ADC governorship primary won by Isah Ashiru. Governor Uba Sani has consequently raised the APC’s Kaduna vote-mobilisation target from two million to three million. This is a campaign objective, not polling evidence. Electoral implications : Kaduna’s opposition organisation is undergoing a significant realignment. The APC has recruited politicians with established connections to the state’s previous administration, while the ADC must assess how the departures affect its ward and constituency structures. They concern the All Progressives Congress (APC) expanding political organisation in Kaduna, fresh local-government election results in Kogi, and an increasingly public disagreement between two major opposition presidential campaigns. 1. KADUNA: PROMINENT EL-RUFAI ALLIES RETURN TO APC Kaduna is in the North-West region. Several former associates of ex-Governor Nasir El-Rufai have defected from the ADC to the APC. They include former Chief of Staff and Finance Commissioner Muhammad Bashir Sa’idu, former Education Commissioner Jafaru Sani and former Senator Suleiman Abdu Kwari. Combo Photo of Uba Sani (L) AND Nasir El-Rufai (R) The defections were formally acknowledged at a reception in Zaria on Saturday, October 17. Sa’idu claims that more than 200,000 ADC members and supporters have moved to the APC. That figure remains an unverified political claim, not an independently established membership count. The departures followed disagreements over the ADC governorship primary won by Isah Ashiru. Governor Uba Sani has consequently raised the APC’s Kaduna vote-mobilisation target from two million to three million. This is a campaign objective, not polling evidence. Electoral implications : Kaduna’s opposition organisation is undergoing a significant realignment. The APC has recruited politicians with established connections to the state’s previous administration, while the ADC must assess how the departures affect its ward and constituency structures. This matters for both the governorship and presidential contests. It does not establish that the defectors’ supporters will necessarily follow them. Kaduna assessment: Organisational alignment materially changed; voter preferences unmeasured. 2. KOGI: APC WINS EVERY LOCAL-GOVERNMENT SEAT A map showing Kogi State The APC has won all 21 chairmanship positions and 239 councillorship seats in Kogi State’s local-government elections conducted on Saturday, October 17. The results were announced on Sunday, October 18, by Mamman Nda-Eri, chairman of the Kogi State Independent Electoral Commission (KOSIEC). The elections covered 21 local government areas and 239 wards. Why this matters The results establish the APC’s control of the elected local-government offices in Kogi. However, these elections were administered by KOSIEC, not INEC. This distinction is important when assessing their significance for the 2027 general elections. State electoral commissions operate under different administrative arrangements from INEC, and local-government elections frequently produce extensive victories for parties controlling state governments. Without detailed turnout figures, ward-level vote totals, opposition participation data and independent observer assessments, the results cannot reliably establish the relative popularity of parties in the forthcoming presidential election. Nevertheless, the outcome provides evidence of the APC’s continuing local-government organisation. Kogi assessment : APC local-government control confirmed; no corresponding presidential voter-strength adjustment. 3. PRESIDENTIAL RACE: KWANKWASO REJECTS WITHDRAWAL FOR ADC Obi (left) and Kwankwaso (right) received their membership cards on Sunday, May 3, 2026. A significant development has emerged in the relationship between the ADC and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). On Sunday, October 18, former Kano Governor Rabiu Kwankwaso, the NDC vice-presidential candidate, declared that the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket would not withdraw in favour of the ADC or another party. He was responding to criticism from the ADC Presidential Campaign Council following his earlier suggestion that ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar should step aside for Peter Obi. The ADC campaign had accused Kwankwaso of undermining opposition unity. President Bola Tinubu’s second-term bid in the 2027 presidential election is being challenged by and opposition leaders. Kwankwaso rejected that accusation and reaffirmed his party’s intention to contest independently. Electoral implications This is relevant to the broader opposition-coalition discussion. The ADC and NDC are presently pursuing separate presidential campaigns. Their public disagreement demonstrates that no unified opposition presidential arrangement has emerged between them. The implications extend particularly to the North-West, where Kwankwaso retains established political networks, and to constituencies where Obi’s 2023 presidential support remains relevant historical evidence. But there is no fresh polling establishing how voters would respond to either cooperation or continued competition. Presidential assessment: Separate ADC and NDC candidatures reaffirmed; no measurable change in voter preferences. THE ELECTORAL MAP : TODAY’S ADJUSTMENTS State/region Development Assessment Kaduna: Former El-Rufai allies move from ADC to APC. Organisational realignment confirmed Kogi APC wins all 260 local-government positions. Local-government control confirmed Kano/North-West: Kwankwaso rejects withdrawal from presidential race; separate NDC campaign reaffirmed Osun/Anambra/Rivers: Existing cross-party presidential arrangements; no additional adjustment Gombe/Ogun Governorship nomination disputes There is no newly verified INEC-conducted election result or credible voter-preference poll requiring a further national assessment. No fresh development establishes a measurable change in support for the PDP, Labour Party, NNPP or significant regional parties. THE BOTTOM LINE This weekend offers three different measures of political strength. Kaduna demonstrates how defections can reshape party organisations. Kogi provides evidence of control over elected local-government offices. And the dispute between the ADC and NDC illustrates the difficulties of coordinating separate presidential ambitions. But none should be mistaken for a reliable prediction of the 2027 election. The important distinction remains between political organisation, electoral participation and actual voter preference. The immediate developments to watch are whether Kaduna’s defections produce verifiable changes in party structures, whether detailed Kogi election data become available, and whether the ADC-NDC disagreement develops into a substantive change in their coalition positions. item.title: VIDEO: Wike Leads Assembly Members, Council Chairmen, Others To Meet With Fubara
item.description: Barely two weeks after an earlier meeting between political leaders loyal to the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, and Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, both camps have held another round of talks aimed at consolidating ongoing reconciliation efforts in the state. Wike led a delegation comprising mainly members of the Rivers State House of Assembly, including its Speaker, Martin Amaewhule, and the 23 local government council chairmen, to meet with Governor Fubara and his supporters at the governor’s private residence in Port Harcourt. Also part of the delegation was the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate in Rivers State, Kingsley Chinda. The latest meeting represents another attempt by the political leaders to build on previous engagements and strengthen efforts to resolve the protracted political crisis that has polarised Rivers State and strained relations between Governor Fubara and members of the State House of Assembly. However, the extent to which the latest meeting will translate into a lasting resolution remains to be seen, amid concerns over the perceived dominance of Wike’s camp in the leadership of the local government councils and the selection of candidates for the 2027 elections, with members of Fubara’s camp seemingly left out of the political arrangements. ﻿ The post VIDEO: Wike Leads Assembly Members, Council Chairmen, Others To Meet With Fubara appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: EPL: Leeds Frustrate Man United To Pile Pressure On Carrick
item.description: Manchester United ended a turbulent week with a frustrating 1-1 draw at Leeds on Sunday that does little to ease the pressure on beleaguered manager Michael Carrick. The Red Devils travelled to the home of their bitter rivals, desperate to find a spark after just two wins in nine games in all competitions this season. The sense of a growing crisis at the club was exacerbated in midweek by an outburst from defender Lisandro Martinez, who took aim at the United hierarchy after a 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. The Argentina centre-back said Carrick, in his first full season in charge at Old Trafford, had been left with an under-strength squad after an underwhelming summer transfer window. The United boss insisted on Friday that United had “moved on” from the incident, and Martinez was named in the starting line-up at Elland Road. Both teams were fully committed in a feisty start to the match in Leeds but there was little goalmouth action. The first effort on target came in the 26th minute when United goalkeeper Senne Lammens clawed away a Nico Elvedi header destined for the top corner after bouncing up off the turf. Bryan Mbeumo, playing as United’s target man, headed wastefully wide a minute later after a fine cross from Youri Tielemans and then shot tamely at Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford. But he finally broke the deadlock in the 35th minute when Tielemans again delivered a low ball from the right which Mbeumo guided into the bottom corner for his fourth Premier League goal of the season. Martinez went off at half-time as Morocco’s Noussair Mazraoui was brought into the action. Leeds started strongly after the break and were level in the 51st minute when Dominic Calvert-Lewin controlled the ball on his chest and finished at full stretch after Tarik Muharemovic got his head to the ball following a corner. item.title: ‘France Is Burning,’ ‘Shattered’ By Immigration, Says Trump
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Sunday blamed immigration for unrest during protests in France and urged the country to tighten its migration rules. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” France was reeling Sunday from widespread damage during protests the day before that, which left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests, piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron six months before elections to replace him. This photograph shows a portion of the partially burnt facade of the Limoges city hall a day after riot and looting following nationwide protests against the “high cost of living” in Limoges on October 18, 2026. PASCAL LACHENAUD / AFP Trump’s post follows similar comments from Vice President JD Vance on Saturday. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this, and they didn’t listen,” Vance wrote on X. “I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he added. Vance, seen as a potential presidential candidate in the 2028 election, also linked it to upcoming midterm races for congressional seats on November 3, where Republicans are not expected to perform well.
